Foreword



Old Sumre is a fictional constructed language, or "conlang", set in a likewise fictional universe, or "conworld" called Torjeo, that I have been pouring my love and effort into for many years. This conlang was among the very first that I constructed when I was a beginner to the art of conlanging, and it is the only one that has survived from that time making it my oldest linguistic creation. While in its early stages it was a crude and poor excuse of a language, it grew with me, the more I learned about languages and the more capable that I became the more nuanced and detailed that Old Sumre became. I can't admit to having filed away every imperfection from those early days as some parts of this language grew on me and became too iconic of the language for me to give up. So if you ever wonder why this language has 20 cases well you now know why.
As Old Sumre has grown in size it has also grown in difficulty with regards to documenting it. For far too long it existed as notes and half finished outdated documents across a variety of platforms, and as of a few years ago, the first Old Sumre dictionary. This book is my attempt to gather every piece of information that exists for this language into one single up-to-date resource. 
Old Sumre is unashamedly my favourite conlang. No other conlang of mine comes close to its sheer size and fleshed out background, nor in effort put into it. This favouritism shines in the fictional world where it lives. There it is viewed by scholars as the perfect language of the far flung Golden Age, ancestral to the languages that dominate its native land. There it is the classical language in which ancient shamans turned scholars first wrote down their poetry and knowledge, their most beloved text being the Sumrichronicon, a compilation of mythical epic poetry spanning the entirety of the Sumric mytho-history from the creation of their world to the compilation of the book. The Sumrichronicon is no mere piece of fiction for it actually exists, or is in the process of existing. As this book is being written I am also working on writing the entirety of the Sumrichronicon in Old Sumre, full of alliterative verse. I hope to one day finish it so that it may be a fitting twin to this book.
In reading this book I hope that whoever reads may find a piece of the same joy that strikes me when making this language, or at the very least be amused by the existence of this beloved bundle of words that I call Old Sumre.
 


The Sumnė People


No description of a language is complete without first telling of its people. Old Sumre was spoken by the Sumnė people, who simply called their language Sumrė. The names of the language and people are both from the verb sumen "to travel" for indeed the Sumnė of the Golden Age were made of populations of nomadic and semi-sedentary people. The language and people described in this book are not those who live in the present day of my world. Rather this book takes you back three thousand years into the Sumric Golden Age, when the continent of Malomanan was still in its own Stone Age. 
The Sumnė, along with the vast majority of "humans" in the Torjeo universe, are not Homo sapiens. In this world the genus Homo has a few living branches, with our kind sapiens making up a measly twig, being confined to an obscure archipelago and isolated from the rest of the human world. In this universe our ancestor Homo heidelbergensis split into two species: Homo sapiens and the fictional Homo spargere. Spargere (from Latin spargere "to scatter, to spread out") is defined by its dull grey skin, large nose, impeccable sense of smell and abundance of hair. The grey skin was an adaption to provide camouflage against the grey and rocky backdrop of an ancient and now flooded continent. When sea levels rose 500,000 years ago it forced populations of spargere to flee across land bridges to dry land. Some of those who couldn't make it fled to mountain tops which then became islands where the people there evolved into Homo spargere pygmeus, a short and stout race of human that is in the process of adapting to ocean life, a hominid analogy to the whale. The fleeing populations spilled into two continents. Those that fled to Henda would adapt to its hot grasslands by losing most of their hair and becoming much more slender, evolving into Homo spargere hendensis. The rest fled to the continent Makutevnag where they remained much the same with the exception of Homo spargere nanus, who adapted to the rainforest by becoming bald all over, incredibly short and skinny with white and brown blotches on their grey skin to blend into the foliage. 
However the homeland of the Sumnė, the continant Malomanan, had yet never known the footstep of a human. It wasn't until 5,000 years ago that the continent was settled by a large number of incredibly lost Nebyetic people from Makutevnag. The Nebyetic people originally spoke a language completely unrelated to Old Sumre and it's kin. The far flung ancestors of the Sumnė were originally Nebyetic hunter-gatherer tribes who sustained themselves off of the forest, speaking an Arhwi-Roquai language called Tagitwi for swathes of time unknown. It wasn't until a population of Sumro-Letaeric newcomers settled in the area that the Nebyetic people interacted with them and abandoned their language for the language of the new people, Proto-Sumro-Letaeric. It is from this language that Old Sumre traces it lineage but even yet some words of that ancient and lost Tagitwi language persisted as substrate vocabulary, as can be seen in the Sumro-Letaeric languages of Malomanan. For example from Tagitwi *snarə wɤt "to rattle vegetation, to push braches aside" comes Old Sumre snernen "to beat, to thrash, to make a loud noise, to warn" and other cognates such as Old Tuura snorti "to trudge through snow", Romoruzian strit "to lead a military campaign" and Red Sucumian snar "to row". The speech of the Nebyetic people would go on to become Proto-Sumro-Naukl, the language of the first lost Nebyetic sea farers to step foot on Malomanan. The descendants of those first pioneers would go on to spread throughout that empty continent and their grey skin lightened over time to compensate for the lacking northern light in their new home. It is to this stock of Homo spargere that the Sumnė belong, along with the Tuuric, Sucumian and Mangeodge peoples.
Over time the ancestors of the Sumnė adapted to the new environment. Unlike their old homeland full of temperate decidious forest, Malomanan offered vast stretches of Taiga forest, chilly grasslands, tundra and towering mountains. The ancestors of the Sumnė led a fully nomadic lifestyle, constantly moving across the land in search of fresh food and water while being aware of the many predators willing to eat them for in this land there are many beasts that our world has long forgotten. Here in Malomanan mammoths, giant sloths, sabre tooth tigers, woolly rhinos and more still live and breathe. Along with that there are a few more otherwordly creatures such as the melodic bull - a species of aurochs gifted with a lyrical language and the giant eagle - a flying fiend that makes easy prey of unaware humans. 
The Sumric Golden Age began when a number of the Sumnė started to live in less mobile communities in a few areas in the south where the predictable food sources encouraged the keeping of food hoards rather than constantly moving. With less mobility people could not worry about accumulating material wealth that would have otherwise weighed them down. Now people could produce art and in time, the literature that gave Old Sumre is revered status of sacred texts. These more settled Sumnė were the voilent and rowdy Afmuud "we who hoard" and the loose bands of nomads who lived like those before were the the pacifist and content Hrotȯngi "footed, with feet". While the culture between these two divisions of Sumnė varied, they both spoke Old Sumre and kept the same myths and stories. The Golden Age came to end when a great plague swept through the continent which devasted the populations of large game. Humans themselves remained uninfected for the most part but with their predictable food source now in tatters they had to change their lifestyle. The Hrotȯngi were quickest to adapt by moving to new areas and taking advantage of alternative food sources. The Afmuud however saw their whole society crumble. No longer could they live in semi-permanent homes or rely on food hoards. The plague forced them to become nomadic once again and to seek other lands and other resources, and with the loss of sedentary life they lost its benefits such as the keeping of art and literature. So began the Dark Ages where literature became scant at best. It wasn't until millenia after the plague that the descendants of the Sumnė, now a wide range of ethnicities speaking a wide range of Old Sumre's descendants, were able to live in settled communities and once again tap into the ancient literature of their Sumnė ancestors, held safe all along in the great underground library Thaighvar far away in the Sucumian Isles. 
The Sumnė of the Golden Age practiced Ška Hwecimsȯne "teaching of origins" or Skawetchimism, a great body of myths and practices relating to the landscape and to the many polytheistic gods and it is in telling these stories that Old Sumre saw it's greatest use.
 


The Old Sumre Language


Old Sumre is a Sumric language, being the ancestor of that branch. It is also a Synrapsian language due to being a daughter language of Proto-Sumric along with Hajec and Old Tuura. The synraspian languages are themselves a branch of the Sumro-Naukl languages, descending from Proto-Sumro-Naukl which is itself a Sumro-Letaeric language descended from Proto-Sumro-Letaeric. The Sumri-Letaeric family is a large one, comprised of 90 languages in the present day. 
Old Sumre possesses many features that were typical of Sumro-Naukl languages of its time: it is Nominative-Accusative with the classic core cases nominative, accusative, genitive and dative, it forms collective nouns via reduplication: rakăt > rakătkăt, and forms the supine with a velar plosive prefix k-: pylen > kpyl "to hew" (cf Old Tuura bolti > gbol, Hajec pol > kpol, Old Mangeodge paluti > cepal, Light Sucumian pəl > kpəu). However despite this the Sumro-Naukl languages can differ quite considerably from each other, being beyond the realms of mutual intelligibility. Even Old Sumre's closest relative at the time, Old Tuura, was too different for them to understand. An example is when a small band of Tuuric raiders would attack coastal villages in the Voro Peninsula (revenge for the Sumnė having brutally invaded and settled it) while dressed as monsters. The raiders would shout olowoji! "run!" as they chased their victims, who, unable to understand Old Tuura mistook the word as the monster's call and after this they named it the Owoloje and so was born the legend of a ferocious sea monster. Had the raiders spoke Old Sumre they would have shouted ñȯmje! and their intentions would have been clearer. What distinguishes Old Sumre the most from its kin is its innovation of its vast case system. Proto-Sumric had a humble four cases but Old Sumre had grammaticalized four vocative cases and twelve locative cases from older postpositions and particles. Not content with that Old Sumre overhauled its noun gender, breaking away from the typical animate-inanimate it innovated two new genders, buzzard and deer, based on the shape of a noun – originally it began as two new declensions but agreement with other parts of speech gave them their gender status. The two new genders went on to dominate Old Sumre's nouns leaving meager scraps to the animate and inanimate genders.
 


Old Sumre Dialects Throughout the Golden Age


This book will paint a very uniform view of Old Sumre and this fairly depicts the reality of the language for most of its existence. With a relatively low population plus frequent moving and mingling with other bands or communities, innovations in the language had high success in spreading throughout the whole population resulting in very little dialectual variation. However the Sumric Golden Age was not devoid of other dialects as towards the end of the Golden Age some dialectual variations started to appear, hinting at the break up of Old Sumrë into the Sumric language family.

The first signs of a distinct dialect forming are found in the 28th Century in the Kingdom of Nusiba. That area is quite remarkable for having a solid monarchy with a fully settled population in a world full of small chieftans and nomads. The Kingdom of Nusiba was founded several centuries prior. Indeed the story of its creation is found in The Book of Man, one of the texts from the Sumrichronicon. The book states that the Kingdom was founded by a man named Dahai who ammased a large army to defeat his human-turned-god brother. When the petty god had been slain the army decided to settle down in the area with Dahai as their king. Ever since then the Nusibna, as they called themselves, lived in relative isolation from the rest of the Sumric world and this was reflected in their speech. This difference was noted by wandering shamans who would often travel through the area and sometimes they would curiously write them down, one such example being the a list written by the shaman Dhoskothos:

 

 

At the time of Dhoskothos's trip to the Kingdom of Nusiba the speech there had began to go through the first sound changes which would eventually lead to the Old Nusibara language. Those changes include syllabic consonants becoming vowel+consonant sequences, lenition of velar plosives before front vowels and the merger of /e o ɔ/ into /a/. The last example even shows the change in marking possessiveness. Instead of using the typical possessive pronouns before a noun (mam ron "my dog") they started adding the dative forms of pronouns as suffixes onto the noun instead. Old Sumrë itself did this but only to mark inalienable possession whereas the Nusiba dialect applied it to all nouns: mam ron > ron mȯ > ranma.

Another dialect that was around in the Golden Age was the dialect that would later become the Alatir language spoken by the Alatin people. The Alatin people descend from Old Sumrë speaking nomads who wandered too far north during the autumn, becoming trapped when the severe winter prevented them from retreating south. Every single nomad there would have frozen to death but a spirit took envy on them and gave them the ability to produce intense heat within themselves to stave off the cold, some could even project the heat to boil water and fewer yet could produce flames and hence the name Alatin, from the Old Sumre Alatinė  "flame people". This gift allowed the nomads to survive in their new northern home. As they lived so far north they lost all contact with the rest of the Sumric world, such so that not a single soul in the south even knew the Alatin existed. The only contact the rest of the Sumnė had with any of the Alatir was on rare occasions when an Alatin would venture far to the south where the people would be in awe of their ability to summon and control fire. The Sumnė did not recognise such people as fellow Sumnė, rather thinking them to be mysterious fire spirits. Thanks to this the Alatin dialect and later the language are completely absent from Sumric literature.

The earliest distinctive feature of the Alatin dialect began with a change in how they marked locative cases. Rather than adding the case endings to the noun itself the Alatin dialect started placing them on pronouns placed after the noun itself: mubenrylė > muben lemyrrlė "on the mountains", ronat > ron lemyrat "to the dog", kugobina > kugo lemyrbin "using an axe". All of these later becoming the Alatir mu̇biu lemiurly, rau lemyrat and küg liurybiu.

The Alatin dialect also experienced a shift in gender marking for some nouns. In Old Sumre inanimate nouns were marked with the suffix -o and animate noun with the suffix -b but the Alatin expanded this so that every noun ending in -o and -b were placed in those genders regardless of what gender they belonged to previously. For example the nouns jamsýro "firewood-DEER", nondo "hat-DEER", skonbo "shaman apprentice-DEER" were all reanalysed as being inanimate O-nouns as can be seen by the change in their inflections, or in these examples, the nominative plural: jamsýrėė > jamsýron, nondėė > nondon, skonbėė > skonbon. Also compare the same phenomenon with nouns ending in -b becoming animate nouns (the examples being in the genitive plural case): knahaban > knahabahė "paranoia-GEN-PL", tilban > tilbahė, hwelagea > hwelagebahė "dear friend-GEN-PL".  An interesting effect of this is that some nouns were then backwards derived based on the reanalysises. So the previously animate Geo-noun hwelageb was reanalysed as the suffix -b attached to the backwards derived noun hwelag "friendship" - really it was derived with the suffix -geb attached to the adjective hwela "fond, nice". Also interesting to note is that the now inanimate noun skonbo referred to a semantically animate entity. This was later "fixed" by making it an animate B-noun: skonbo > skaub > skaub-ba > skaubba.

The Alatin dialect went through several sound changes during the Golden Age. These include:

 

  •  The epenthesis of /j/ before word initial vowels when a consonant cluster followed.
    • anso > janso "white", obwitan > jobvitan "burden"
  • Syllabic consonants becoming /iC/ sequences.
    • khɫd > khild "disease", kmegɫ > kmegil "performing"
  • /w/ becoming /v/.
    • welna > venla "underground", wúddra > vuudra "kayak".
  • The sequences /rt tr/ and /rd dr/ becoming /t͡ʃ/ and /d͡ʒ/.
    • waatre > vaace "pleasant", vürrtutren > vücucen "to listen to music".
  • Metathesis where coda /Vr/ becomes /rV/ when after a velar plosive, or becoming /NV/ when not after a velar plosive.
    • uklyrsȯn >uklrysȯn "simply, just", gar > gra "sorrow".
    • vdomir > vdommi "mental", unsivartšen > unsivmatšen "to get ready".
  • Short vowels lengthening before geminate consonants, with said consonants then shortening.
    • nudda > nuuda "lizard", fjáddra > fjaača "eider duck".
  • Umlaut occurring where the vowels /ʌ a i u o ɔ/ become /ɛ ɛ e ʏ ø œ/ when the next syllable has /e/. This especially affected the nominative plural.
    • ronė > rynė "dogs", ansėė > jensėė "white-DEER.NOM.PL"

As well as dialectual differences that began during the Golden Age, there were a few differences that date back to the Late Proto-Sumric period. 

Old Sumre, as spoken by the nomadic Hrȯtongi, differed little from the language spoken by the settled Afmuud however there were some key differences:

  • Proto-Sumric *r never became n before consonants like it did in Afmuud Old Sumre (albeit quite sporadically):
    • PS *aβlǒrβ "cruel" > OS ablon, Hrȯtongi OS ablyr
    • PS *ərtaa "east" > OS ӑntė, Hrȯtongi OS yrtė
    • PS *beśβ "equipped with" > *berβ > OS -bin "prolative case ending", Hrȯtongi Old Sumre -bir
    • PS *aźblə- "for the sun to shine" > *arblə- > OS amblen, Hrȯtongi OS arblen
  • Proto-Sumric *ġ is preserved as j word initially, and as i post-vocalically, rather than being lost initially and lengthening the previous vowel when post-vocalic (or lost when word final after a vowel):
    • PS *ġǒrənats "rotten, expired > OS yrnac "sour", Hrȯtongi OS jyrnac
    • PS *ġaʔtǒlda "squint, bent, indirect" > OS áttylda "oblique, indirect, vague", Hrȯtongi OS játtylda
    • PS *ġəʔxuv- "to tug, to snatch, to grab" > OS *ӑkuven "to tear, to rip", Hrȯtongi OS jӑkuven
    • PS *ělkuġlǒ "mountain stream" > OS elaküülo "gland, pore, water source", Hrȯtongi OS elakuilo
    • PS *aġəl "sparse" > OS ėl "rare, uncommon", Hrȯtongi OS ail
    • PS *bəsaġənpa "pole" > OS bsėnpa "pole, shaft, handle", Hrȯtongi OS bsainpa
    • PS  *daġa "now" > OS dėa, Hrȯtongi OS daja
    • PS *arəsətroġ "sign, warning" > OS arstare "wave", Hrȯtongi OS arstarȯi
  • The sporadic merger of Proto-Sumric *s *z to f v, and *s to t did not occur:
    • PS *ǒsja "bread > OS otja, Hrȯtongi OS osja
    • PS nijǒs "grass"> OS *nilaf, Hrȯtongi OS nilas
    • PS *jǒz- "to smile" > OS laven, Hrȯtongi OS lasen

The Old Sumre spoken in Pehpema (Modern day northern Vitsoresh) lacked preaspiration altogether due to turning Proto-Sumric *xC into geminate CC rather than ʰC: PS *axte "hand, palm" > OS ahti "paw", Pehpema OS atti "paw"; PS *poxpě "inland" > OS pehpe Pehpema OS peppe (indeed, people from Pehpema called their region Peppema).

Quite conversely, the Puhma dialect turned PS *ʔC into preaspirated consonants rather than geminates, with *ʔw *ʔx *ʔ clusters becoming hw hj h: PS *eʔbě "afterlife" > OS íbbe, Puhma OS íhbe; PS *ġǒsətronseʔwə- "to touch" > OS ostrensígen, Puhma Old Sumre ostrensíhwen; PS *gəwʔxə "goo, slime" > OS gowk "ooze, puss, goo", Puhma Old Sumre gow.

After the Golden Age when settled populations were forced to become nomadic and seek alternative lifestyles, the Pehpema and Puhma dialects were both wiped out as their speakers intermingled heavily with the rest of the Old Sumrë speaking world. However some dialect loans occured and survive into modern Sumric languages today. Speakers of Puhma Old Sumrë tended to move east, some reaching so far east that they, along with people from Photma and Skarma, became the ancestors of the first Old Moca speakers which is evidenced by a handful of Old Moca words coming from Puhma forms:

  • Old Moca ẹ̄ve < Puhma íhbe  - the variant íbbe would have become *ẹ̄be
  • Old Moca gʷuć < Puhma gowh - the variant gowk would have become *gʷuk
  • Old Moca ekẹ̄vus < Puhma akíhwos - the variant akíkkjos would have become ekẹ̄jus
  • Mocha dẹ̄ver < Puhma dishwar - the variant disgar would have become dẹ̄ger

Some speakers of Pehpema Old Sumre ventured south to Nusiba, where they assimilated into the Old Nusibara speaking population although a few of their own words were loaned into Old Nusibara:

  • Old Nusibara at "dog's paw" < Pehpema atti "paw" - the form ahti became Old Nusibara ahti
  • Old Nusibara pepe "by land" < Pehpema peppe "inland"  - the form pehpe became Old Nusibara pehpi "inland"

The Hrȯtongi dialect had a better fate, as it survived and went on to become Middle Sumri, the language spoken by all Sumric nomads right after the Golden Age, in time becoming the six Middle Sumric languages. 

Phonology

Vowels

 

Old Sumre also has the diphthongs <ow ĕi ėi ăo> /ɔʊ̯ ɜi̯ ei̯ ʌo̯/.

Word finally [ʌ] is not permitted. Rather in this position it breaks into the sequence [au]. [ʌ] may find itself in a word final position when certain prefixes are added, such as the suffix s- which denotes the young of a species, which delete all but the first two syllables: atăbi "monster" > satau "brat". As a long vowel [ʌː] may occur, mostly in the accusative plural of deer nouns: raalistӑӑ "flood-ACC.PL.DEER".

The short schwa [ə̆] serves only to exist as an epenthetic vowel between the word final clusters /rn rm lm/. This epenthetic vowel does not affect the placement of the mobile pitch accent and it is not written.

Fronting

The back vowels [u o ʌ ̴ɔ] front to [ʏ ø œ] when before the consonants /l r/. Despite being allophonic this change in vowel quality is shown in the orthography. 

There do exist however a decent amount of exceptions to this rule, most of which tend to be proper nouns, mostly theonyms.

This fronting of the back vowels only occurs when the vowel is within three syllables of the end of a word. When the vowel is made to be in a syllable further left than that, usually by compounding or suffixation, then it reverts back to its back vowel quality in a process termed back vowel restoration. Since both /ɔ/ and /ʌ/ front to [œ], when [œ] reverts to a back vowel it becomes either /ɔ/ and /ʌ/. Which vowel it reverts to is notated in the dictionary as it is otherwise unpredictable to know.

This fronting also does not happen when followed by a word final plosive. When this plosive is rendered non-final, via compounding or suffixation, the vowel then becomes affected by fronting. A very common example of this is the divine suffix -olk.

Of these vowels /ʏ œ/ exist as phonemes in other words, due to /ʏ/ coming from Proto-Sumric *ü /ʉ/ and /œ/ coming from Proto-Sumric *ɘ̈ /ɵ/ which arose from an earlier *o *ö when affected by the umlaut triggered by *ü.

The instance of Proto-Sumric *munjə becoming Old Sumr byñ is quite an irregular change given that in no other word did *u become /œ/. As will come to be seen, Old Sumre is speckled with such sporadic sound changes.

Diphthongs

The diphthongs of Old Sumre are ow ĕi ėi ăo /ɔʊ̯ ɜi̯ ei̯ ʌo̯/ and of these ow is the only  "inert" diphthong as it does not become a vowel+approximant sequence like the others when before vowels.

Umlaut

Old Sumre has an umlaut which remains productive in affixes (such affixes are listed with a superscript ᵘ for reference) which is triggered by phonemic ü. The umlaut originated in Late Proto-Sumric, as observed by the lack of umlaut in Hajik which is from Early Proto-Sumric, when the rounded central vowel *ü began affecting the vowels in adjacent syllables. When *ü occurred in an adjacent syllable it caused high rounded vowels to centralise to *ü, high-mid vowels to centralise to *ɘ̈ [ɵ] and low-mid vowels to centralise to [ə]. The front unrounded vowels [i e ɛ] where rounded to [y ø œ]. The diphthongs /aʊ əʊ~oʊ/ became /əʉ ɵʉ/.

*This pattern of /i/ becoming /o/ is no longer a productive mutation, rather it is for words formed with umlaut in the Late Proto-Sumric period which had /e/ become /ø/. Since there was a merger in Old Sumrë where /e/ raised to /i/, the vowel /i/ could mutate to either /u/ or /o/. Analogy quickly ensured that all /i/ would mutate only to /u/. However there are some words which show traces of the /i/>/o/ umlaut when it occured in Proto-Sumric such as pič "digging tool" and počtü "prairie dog" coming from Proto-Sumric *pedź and *pödźtü. This word in particular is a great example of the analogy that occured as in Old Sumrë the same suffix -tüᵘ was applied to the same root but it resulted in the newer /i/>/u/ umlaut: pič > pučtü "armadillo".

Consonants


 Allophony

  • Long consonants shorten when a long vowel follows.
    • meelgüllen [mɛ̀ːlɡʏ́lːɛn] "to teach" > meelgülaa [mɛ̀ːlɡʏ́laː] "I teach"
    • plétta [plɛ́tːa] "branch" > pletėė [plɛ́teː] "branches"
  • The nasal /m/ becomes the voiceless [m̥] when before a preaspirated consonant.
    • ramhpo /rámʰpɔ/ [rám̥pɔ] "alliteration"
  • When long and before a preaspirated consonant, the nasal becomes [m͡m̥].
    • nemmhko /nɛ́mːʰkɔ/ [nɛ́m͡m̥kɔ] "slave"

Proto-Mangeodge (*mangēoǰar̄os) was a Sumro-Naukl language spoken between circa 600-1600AN. It is a direct descendant of Proto-Sumro-Naukl and it is considered to be one of the earliest offshoots to diverge away from Proto-Sumro-Naukl. Proto-Mangeodge was spoken in the "Old South" region of Meilvarestu before spreading to the "Great Middle" region sometime around 1000AN. The speakers of Proto-Mangeodge were early agriculturalists, the pioneers of agriculture in Malomanan in fact. Towards the later stages of the Proto-Mangeodge period the Mangeodge kingdoms had developed and military technology improved drastically. A lot of the "pre-Unification" of Mangeodge history was when Proto-Mangeodge was spoken. Of course all of that history was passed down via oral history due to there being no contemporary written records. When that history finally was written down, it was done so in Old Mangeodge. Proto-Mangeodge was not completely unwritten however. In fact it was the first language in Malomanan to be written in using the first script to be found in Malomanan: the Celos Alphabet. The Celos alphabet first appeared in the 14 Century (around 4,800 years ago) in Meilvarestu where it was devised by some speakers of Proto-Mangeodge to carve writing onto standing stones, although surviving written examples are very rare hence why the language is very much unattested. The surviving inscriptions are to be found on ancient border stones which were erected around border areas to mark territory but also to fend away evil spirits from the outside and the inscriptions convey this intent e.g:

Verbs

SS-Verbs

SS-Verbs are verbs derived with the reflexive causative suffix -ess, either within Old Mangeodge or during an earlier stage; awipeissti "to excrete, to shit, to poo, to defecate, to fart, to smell bad, to stink". Even if these verbs have no true semantic patient, they are obligated to have the subject also be the direct object, and this is marked using the appropriate pronoun in the oblique case; awipeisssik maseju "I farted" (lit "I farted me"). The semantic patients of SS-Verbs are treated as syntactic indirect objects following the post-position vaelauk "by, using, with": jarucdeizi cabeitessacc iameleju orunvotaisoteiju vaebauk "The master taught the apprentice" (lit "The master taught him(self) with the apprentice").

There are SS-verbs whose meanings do not appear to be truly reflexive, such as awipeissti, this is because they were coined before the Old Mangeodge period and semantic change has occured - for example awipeissti comes from Proto-Sumro-Naukl *ahaxüpe-əδs "to empty oneself" (cf Old Mangeodhe awipei "barren, sterile") and padessti "to drink water" comes from Proto-Sumro-Naukl *pad-əδs "to make oneself wet".

Derivational Morphology

Defunct and Archaic Morphemes

This section will serve to point out derivational morphology that was once productive in the ancestors of Lanwurq but are no longer so in Lanwurq itself, now being non-productive remnants.

  • a-; found in prepositions, verbs and adverbs. From Old English a-, on- "in, on, at" - as a prefix often denoted motion away from.
    • abhach "aloof, away, behind" (cf bach "back"), abhé "to suffer for", abhíh "at a distance, aside, away from others", abhijd "to remain faithful to, to adhere to" (cf bijd "to stay"), abhún "above", abhúq "about", abréd "widely" (cf bréd "broad"), abríd "to spread abroad, to spread widely", abríst "side by side" (cf bríst "breast")
  • be-; found in verbs. From Middle Scots be- "derives transitive verbs from intransitive verbs" < Old English be- < Proto-Germanic *bi- "by".
    • bednc "to decorate", befo "to befall" (cf fo "to fall"), beghnc "to cheat in a relationship, to be unfaithful,  to fool, deceive, jilt, stupefy", beghúf "to begin, to start", beghých "to jilt, to beguile, to betray, to cheat, to swindle", beheht "to promise, to vow", behod "to behold" (cf hod "to hold"), belauing "to belong", bemín "to denigrate, to degrade, to humiliate, to demoralise", besích "to beseech" (cf sích "to find, to seek"), beswích "to beguile, to allure, to trick", beteh "to put in trust, to entrust" (cf tach "to take"), bewitch "to enchant, to turn sour", bewév "to cause to waver, to shield", befañchiq "grace, graced" (via the past participle of the Middle Scots beþank "to thank")
  • -oñ; found in adjectives. From Old English -ol, -el "derives adjectives from verbs, denoting inclination or tendency toward" < Proto-Germanic *-ilaz, *-ulaz "agentive suffix" < Proto-Indo-European *-lós or *-dʰlom/-tlom.
    • brichoñ "brittle, fragile, crumbly, easily broken" (cf brech "to break")
  • -oñ; found in verbs and some noun. From Old English -lian "frequentive verb suffix" from Proto-Germanic *-lōną, perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *-ulaz.
    • añqoñ "to nag", bebhoñ "to sip quickly", bibhoñ "bubble", biqoñ "mallet, masher", bohhoñ "old shoe, odd thing, clumsy person, to distort, to disfigure, to warp", braqoñ "clatter, gunshot, peal, thunder, noise of a horse’s hoofs, spell of bad weather, to make a clattering noise""

","title":"Añdrachlís in ilijn: Andracles and the Lion","translation":"

A slave was in Rome for the first time, and they call him Andracles. The master was a cruel person, and he was too cruel to Andracles, such that he ran away to the end. He hid each day in the wild forest, but he could find no food. He slowly got so sick and so weak that he prepared to die. He entered a cave a while later, he crouched and then slept deeply. Not long after, a horrible noise woke him up. A lion entered the cave and began to roar loudly. Andracles was very afraid. He was sure that the lion would kill him. He understood quickly that the lion was not angry, it limped as if it has a sore foot. He then grew braver so he took the top of lion's limping foot to see what was wrong with him. The lion stood as quietly as a sheep and rubbed its head against the man as if it wanted to say \"I know that you'll help me\". Andracles lifted the foot and saw that there was a long and sharp splinter. He grabbed the end and pulled it out with his finger. The splinter was removed. The lion got so happy that it started leaping like a dog, liking its new friend very much. Because of this, Andracles was not afraid. He lay down and slept next to the lion when it got dark. The lion brought something for Andracles to eat. Thus, Andracles became friends with the lion, such that he became healthier. Then the soldiers went to the woods and found Andracles in the cave. They recognised him and took him back to Rome. According to the laws of that time, a slave who ran away fought with a hungry lion. According to those laws, they trapped him with a hungry lion and waited for the right hour. When that day came, thousands of people came to gather and see. The people saw such sights that are modest today in circuses or football games. They opened the door, they brought poor Andracles through. The poor man was very afraid, he could already hear the lion roaring. He looked up, he did not see the sadness in thousands of the faces that were around him. Then the hungry lion ran to him. He reached the poor man with one leap. Andracles called loudly not out of fear but with happiness. He recognized his friend from the cave. The people who waited for the lion to kill the man already were very confused. The way that Andracles hugged the lion's neck, the way that he lay in front of him, the way that they licked with love, the way that the slave cuddled with him, as if he asked him to pet him, and nothing was misunderstood. They slowly began to ask for everything to be explained, Andracles stood while embracing the lion's neck, to say how they lived together in the cave. \"I am a person\", he said, \"I did not find a friend amongst people, just this poor lion which is nice to me, it's why I love him as a brother\". Now the people could not be cruel to the poor slave. \"Live and be free!\" they called. \"Let them be free and give freedom to the lion too!\" a second one called. Thus Andracles was free and they gave freedom to the lion also. It is said that they lived in Rome together for many years.

AUQMAQNG fe ood lauing sijn!

Híar, nósín gadabhúqje! Lóras frusoñs burlije!; híar, ighlens winje, quhiq ilughemi saqjelíniq fur? Inóníst burnsís gyos amneherqngðm! Ichlarsahs súan fe istén amneherqngiq! Cumje Lúas wijfehiñqije in íssyo críjeiq bach te ibhéard. Ilóhs Lóhôn amluiqng qeiq furiq, qe imurc óme Úfórnas furf, quhor þiq Fingoñs dúñchmn fe isí, fe iwns gyo. Þursne muchuo eichañphijns fe Móvn in anócheñq laan!

Alódaghadje Starnó eseñqm furFngoñ qesphíarm furidijiq qechm qeiq; ibhijghón ichíng emijnídiq biq we oísangur iqbaccm. \"Nó ín Górmuos móse túars, Nó ín Starnóm Fingoñm íonesíðm. Idífsr dunurin er ísfijure syo se schadas! Jon bór manómijniniq? Ichíngsís quhijqhaaníd dóhtur? Gije Lódas sinje; íswurtsr se iwn qe Fingoñ: iwn þiqs drijfn ifrusoñ in hérsts murce ghlen abhúq. Dúmarúnam, idífs éarym! Crómaghlasm, eiéarn téardjís! Strúmórm, istúars feðrums stijur! Crómarm þiq ísschipsr etlin ón isís we nén eifaschn se afijureflóhts eqlin, ón murc in burlin clúts! Tóvjís abhúqmi ichañphijñsís wéñsjís! in a laan þiqsne ceñq! Iocajn liqjísðm furístéardj qeluich iqiq se Treñmór, iwaarsís ringur. \"Dúñchmje\" se Treñmór esés, \"stijije þiqs ichlarsahs atwíñðm! Is bhurn jemngariq fur qeawobhuroñ, ur qewala wemi in ierd.\"

Imuin itóviq erðm se bréd!

To Dúmarúnam echm we iéarymsem: fe istéñsís Cróma, ighots fron hiñqurm! Etóviq ón iswos in ísmurc bóq quhin þiq iqswid Crúmórma egharqiq fur qewaqng. Es'chañst quhijoñs þiq ewstchésn, amauing inófríans: Nén ifíarws júars Dúmarúnaje!

\"Daare Cyos sinje, wimafiqduñts bi furiq ben iniht? Oñaerluicðm fe is téardj er þurscañse chlañs? Starnó ilóhsís cíngms afórmi, in Swaraanm inócheñqjns nófrían. We Lódas stén eismeðm þurwurtsrne fur nuhn. Íswijf schudbi lénurle seghn se þiq Dúmarúnadne bagge, quhor þiq two bichurin burnsr djijnin ón Cramócrylas fórist. Ihiosr abhúq, we idurlin wits; isís gyon níst. Ighyon gús masns erluiqngðm, ajng dunurur ón itían. Ighots híd gísjeiq qe Cañdóna, teojeum aneñq ísféðurs blijfnis, quhin þiq Úfórnas djaghe smeðm iqburoñq ón ísliftiq lístur. Maacs in iwaar teojeum aneñqðm! Teojeum quhor þiq ísda edíd!\"

\"Nó nómeñsfe aneñq maféðurs,\" Fingoñ esés, \"ben isís aeqoñq. In iood lauing sijn þurtijmswur aneñq inóchanenis. Imurcnisisne staanin óñmi, inófríans afórðm, junge in ihaaremi bit. Cramócrylas ringije, inihts tíans mijns.\"

Fingoñ erun we imuchuo faschn we ijéarymeum ben iniht, fúlyqm er Túrórs burn þiq iqshy gyo iqseñqiq, ben Górmuos haare ghlen. Astén amuiñsbhór iqscañst óniq; in imid awihte fórm iqstaaníd; afórym þiq ibhlone haar iqhudit, se Lóhôns quhijqbrístiq lasís. Urfiqduñqsr nómach in þurcuqe. Abrechiq sauing schísfronjn ón iwn. Iquhijq éarymseur schísmuifnðm aft fur þiq idúos stijn in ursyo.

\"Tórcuotórnaje, we iwalan haar\" schisés, \"quhorabhúqs ijurfiqduñts nú, we Lúon? Jetijñq iq jurén murc burns, Cóñbncarglas daje! Amsínje biq, Lúons ringije, dafn bi Lódas ho, quhin þiq imurc niht aqsiqburoñq ben is'chí. Imuin jurhijdniq jurtéardj jésnjeiq aft. Asínr se nóbriht bín, in Eofn. Ihaarije jursuiñðm erte ifijureflóhts qebhi, in jurron alauing iniht. Quhiq manómijníd fur?, in mawím, ihaare ghotsís cíngje. Úqluicje fe Lódas ho, it jurlenurle dóhtur.\"

\"Quho sjurseo,\" Fingoñ esés, \"inihts vijs?\"

Schiawobhuroñq quhijoñs þiq schiwsschúghen.

\"Quho sjurseo, in jurmurcnis?\"

Schiscriñchoñq qe iwím.

Itos þiq ihañseur iqfiroñq ichíng echiqiq. Esphíarqr urféðurs aneñqðm.

\"Tórcuotórna,\" schises, \"estijd iq Lúons slo bhurn: estijd, nú biq, icrín schao ísschúgheniq. Atrist ehudjn we Starnó eLóhôn in iwaar; imurcíd cíngs þefóht fur lauing sijn. Madam edíd, in ibhluidem, Tórcuotórnam we ibhlé téardj! Ifischísecs adjaghiqðm quhijoñs þiq awsbi astén iq Lúons burn. Ihaaremi iquhijq haanemi iqhéñq affe ifaschn wns. Adn aherciñqjn. Iínemiwur waare. Isaft brístemi tóviq híh. Mafiqduñqswur furiq, iq Lúon, furatrist qehéjn wije, Tórcuotórnaje. IqwsStarnó, io cíngm! Ísrid ín þebhuroñq óñmi we iló. Íshaare brú iqschúghíd murc, íssmurc wurfiq abhún. Quhor smada, asés, aqm þiqws se mihte in iwaar! Jurdngíd lénurle amauing inófríans, Tórcuotórnas dóhtije! Ihaanemi efangiqiq. Iséo agharqiq fur qetóv. Is wím eiñphiqmi murc. Se ahéñq haar ísijchmn. Maféðurs téardj ísijlifnniq afórmi. Ameñs eijngnisis ijghon ben far fe mawím. Starnós sins fliqn in masiht. Ísstijn lénurle in masyo.\"

\"Lúons lasije,\" Fingoñ esés, \"idúos quhijqhaaníd dóhtije! Achlúd þiqs brinoñq we ifijurs burlin ben masyo. Jon murc cléft muin deñ luicje qeiq; þé fijureflóht fe Eofn deñ luicje qeðm. mas'chañse flíarischis abhúqje, manófríñsís fíar! 'Sneiwécjnsís flíarisch, 'snefe imurcnis in isyo ano! Ilasísrne firoñq in urwíms ebhurns! Iquhijq éarymseðm þurnemuifnðm lénurle. þurburlin sónse we ihaareðm, abhún Seomas clarsahs. Ivijsíseðmsne in iwuo desurq. Wurcúare ben isónse súan!\"

Ísfiqduñts egharqðm fur furiqur qebhi anen, bréd ben inihts bríst, qe quhor þiq Lódas tren þeschúghíd in ibhlyq. Frí sténs we idóts eimósr þer; abhurn we abhichurin eqlin, buroñq abhúqðm, sich se 'sLódas imurc rid clúd. Aghést iqluichiq furiq fe iqstaq híh, haf fórymd fe ischadae duñq. Ísvijs ephuiarqiq ben ighyon burn aft. Íswurts two cañphijns þeghóqðm níst, burlin unur acruichiq trí, in Starnó, inócheñqjnsís nófrían. Þehíod ón þurbrúan téardjís: þurlístursr furiq ben iniht. Starnós blone bhíarts murcnisis gyon frihtfe.

Fingoñs fiqduñqs þeherciñqðm. Isodjurs þetóviq we þurwaqms. \"Swaraanje, garje furþon dunurur furlo qebhi,\" Starnó esés we íssmeðm. \"Jurdas téardj tacjeiq. 'Sasten in iwaar.\" Íss'chañse lístur Swaraanm efroniq. Itstaaníd fast in Lódas trí. Þin inófríans þechm furiq we þurswearts. Þurdne flíarisch þemeoqíd. Lúnas my dingiq ben Swarañs téardjís firlins. Itéardj iqfon, burlin ón ierd. Ibhniq iqfon se dingiq. Iliftiq flíarisch Fingoñ estaphiqiq. Swaraan staaníd angurq, nóérmiq. Icwéq ínem ebhuroñq; íssweard efroniq qe ierd. Þin equhusoñq se þiq ibhurn eerluichiqiq slo.

Swarañs nó sín bi ísda. Starnós awobhurlin we iradj. Ihaare brúseum þewur murc abhún íshéñq angurnnis. Lódas trí ísdngniq íslístur jénsneiq. Isangsís din ísgharinðm furlúdur qebhi. Lóhôn þurcumn qeiq, iocajn we ísén murc géq; se two burlin burn þiqr fe two puiarne ghlens! Túrórs fórist Fingoñ ebhaggéd qeiq. Iésts liht iqtóviq sónse. Lóhôns buts iqscañst óñðm in ichíngs haan. Tórcuotórnas dóhtur schiúqcm fe iwím we siqng bónenis. Ihaarer fe iwn schihéñqiq. Ursauing schifútóviqiq wuo. Ischaosís Lúons sauing, quhor þiq urda estijd. Starnó bluide téardj schisíniq. Aliht ibhlijfnis iqtóviqiq ón ichúqmer. Swarañs dingiq buniq schisíniq. Schiscriñchoñq murc fe Fingoñ. \"Saqjedíd bi ahnur ejurburns?, Lóje fe idúle lase?\"

In iwaqur tóvnje Úfórnaje! Quhos sijd sinihts fijureflóhts ón? Imurc muin þiqs dúñchmn ahijn jurósm wits amsíniq. Ihaare Lódas stijn ón jurtaq: Miñsís eofs hús! Crúlódas eisweartsis buroñq dubhoñ in íschlúde hos en. Ísfóryms sín nóef ben ísóme haar. Ísriht hañs ón ístéardj. Inósihtfe schaos in ís'chear haan. ísósm hos ruifs brinoñq we nihte fijurs!

Crúlódas cinr cumn furiq, arigh efórymlis schadas. Icrín schao ísracsn qe þéðm þiq iwaar þes'chañst iniq. Se amurc bo ístéardjis tóvn, atwínm in iwécjns biq. Ísafon fijureflóht te iwéchiq érmitjns. Lúons quhijqbrístiq lase schichm se briht se aflo ón ibhurns.

","title":"Óschn: Ossian","translation":"

Fingal when very young, making a voyage to the Orkney Islands, was driven by stress of weather into a bay of Scandinavia, near the residence of Starno, king of Lochlin. Starno invites Fingal to a feast. Fingal, doubting the faith of the king, and mindful of a former breach of hospitality, refuses to go. Starno gathers together his tribes; Fingal resolves to defend himself. Night coming on, Duth-maruno proposes to Fingal to observe the motions of the enemy. The king himself undertakes the watch. Advancing towards the enemy, he accidentally comes to the cave of Turthor, where Starno had confined Conban-Cargla, the captive daughter of a neighbouring cheif. Her story in imperfect, a part of the original being lost. Fingal comes to a place of worship, where Starno, and his son Swaran, consulted the spirit of Loda concerning the issue of war. The recounter of Fingal and Swaran. Duan first concludes with a description of the airy hall of Cruth-Ioda, supposed to be the Odin of Scandinavia. The bards distinguished those compositions in which the narration is often interrupted by episodes and apostrophes, by the name of Duan. A TALE of the times of old! Why, though wanderer unseen! thou bender of the thistle of Lorna; though breeze of the valley, hast thou left mine ear? I hear no distant roar of streams\" No sound of the harp from the rock! Come, thou huntess of Lutha, Malvine, call back his soul to the bard. I look forward to Lochlin of lakes, to the dark billowy bay of U-thorno, where Fingal descends from ocean, from the roar of winds. Few are the heroes of Morven in a land unknown! Starno sent a dweller of Loda to bid Fingal to the feast; but the king remembered the past, and all his rage arose. \"Nor Gormal's mossy towers, nor Starno, shall Fingal behold. Deaths wander, like shadows, over his fiery soul! Do I forget that beam fo light, the white-handed daughter of kings? Go, son of Loda; his words are wind to Fingal; wind, that, to and fro drives the thistle in autumn's dusky cale. Duth-maruno, arm of death! Cromma-glas, of Iron shields! Struthmor, dweller of battle's wing! Cromar, whose ships bound on seas, careless as the course of a meteor, on dark-rolling clouds! Arise around me, children of heroes, in a land unknown! Let each look on his shield like Trenmor, the ruler of wars. \"Come down,\" thus Trenmor said, \"thou dweller between the harps! Thou shalt roll this stream away, or waste me in earth\". Around the ing they rise in wrath. No words come forth: they sieze their spears. Each soul is rolled into itself. At length the sudden clang is waked on all their echoing shields. Each takes his hill by night: at intervals they darkly stand. Unequal bursts the hum of songs, between the roaring wind! Broad over hem rose the moon! In his arms came tall Duth-maruno: he, from Croma of rocks, stern hunter of the boar! In his dark boat he rose on waves, when Crumthormo awaked its woods. In the chase he shone, among foes: No fear was thine. Duth-maruno! \"O Son of daring Cromhal, shall my steps forward through the night? From this shield shall I view them, over their gleaming tribes? Starno, king of lakes, is before me, and Swaran, the foe of strangers. Their words are not in vain, by Loda's stone of power. Should Duth-maruno not return, his spouse is lonely at home, where meet two roaring streams on Crathmocraulo's plain. Around are hills, with echoing woods; the ocean is rolling near. My son looks on screaming sea-fowl, a young wanderer on the field. Give the head of a boar on his lifted spear. Tell him of my deeds in war! Tell where his father fell!\".  \"Not forgetful of my fathers,\" said Fingal, \"I have bounded over the seas. Theirs were the times of danger in the days of old. Nor settles darkness on me, before foes, though youthful in my locks. Chief of Crathmocraulo, the field of noght is mine\". Fingal rushed, in all his arms, wide bounding over Turthor's stream, that sent its sullen roar, by night, through Gormal's misty vale. A moonbeam glittered on a rock; in the midst stood a stately form; a form with floating locks, like Lochlin's white-bosomed maids. Unequal are her steps, and short. She throws a broken song on wind. At times she tosses her white arms: for grief is dwelling in her soul. \"Torcal-tonro, of aged locks,\" she said, \"where now are thy steps, by Lulan? Though hast failed at thine own dark streams, father of Conban-cargla! But I behold thee, chief of Lulan, sporting by Loda's hall, when the dark-skirted night is rolled along the sky. Though sometimes hidest the moon with thy shield. I have seen her dim, in heaven. Though kindlest thy hair into meteors, and sailest along the night. Why am I forgot, in my caave, king of shaggy boars? Look from the hall of Loda, on the lonely daughter\".

Sún Tsú esés:

Waars amétur emuchuo nídn te imuchuotín; 'siéart elijf ur díf; 'sighét fur ifóon ur itijnin. 'Snídit furit tebhi léarnt bro.

  • Lí Tchúan: \"Watmsr tuios eiio wíard\". Waars afóhte faschn; juríare gin þit mincañeghe ónit nó we ihiñtng aneñtit ermuchuo.

In se, véojijeit we ifijf muchuo péarts in macjeðm abhísns eisívn péarts þitr gíd néms eftur. Se þit itsnídithngwís jemiht tedjalúsðm.

Ifórmést eís phéartsr uncaghidnise intach; inísnnjns iwíður, ifurts ilaan, ifyarts ibhidn; in ififts iléarnin.

  • Thauing Jú: iórdnur wij þits abhúns féar strehtfurit. Quhin isódjursr liftit fuririú teghíit teðm ifangurs, ienjúhnis eiringurs gidnis in icrúsnis eþurfóch ichurcecúñsoñs djalúsnit fórmést; nísnn, nétchurs sésns rihnnis, in hinmést iséarnis eilaan. Eftur hiú hiñtng aneñt ifrí eís méturs agrífs gart furistítng teaghn. Eftur iméartchís isódjurs atsðmgéd er, ipheñsenis ón igrív.

We i-ncaghidnis ntach, at þits garin ifóch tebhi éwcuoécwuo we þurringurs ametlin, se þit þuoge weðm in lijf in te díf nó we ifíar edífs nóchanenis.

  • Tchauing Jú: Quhin ighidnis, idjóních in irihnnis jurgíñðm te ifóch, in quhin icrúsnis jurgínit teðm anen, iéarmeo bi djiñjt we imijn in ébdeo bi blijf furþurringurs tehertng teðm. ibhuich etchingís itsés: \"We ibhlijfnis fe winin aneñst þur séarnisís, inóchanenis edíf fócr ijnómijnin.\"

We iwíður, nétruo hingwís beñseos ametlin; iténawo ewínturs coodnis in esmurs warymnis in iéarmís déns we écwuoécwuo we isésns.

We ilaan, ileñfs ametlin, quhíður igruns véghit ben ef ur séar, quhíður 'sótm ur tiht, in icheps elijf ur edíf.

  • Mij Jiú-tchen:...Quhin isódjurs jurhénin, 'snídit furiéarts in péarts eilaan techeñ. Quhijoñs ileñfs jechceñ, anóstreht ur streht plój jecnjés. gin þit ibhúch eiefnis ur séarnis fe ilaan véghn echeñs þin ibhetur fe fitesódjurs ur hórsesódjurs jésn ecndjalúsit. gin þit quhor igruns tiht in clós in quhor 'sótm echeñs þin ibhúch eiéarme þits nídit ecndjalús. gin þit quhor istúar íogíit echeñs þin quhin furíséarme tehén ur teschéo echeñs.

We ibhidn, igrífs tracs fe iwijt, isuifasnnis, ilíonis, ismeðm in suiarnis ametlin.

  • Lí Tchúan: ifijf eísr igrífs grésenis. Se þit iéarmí þechonm \"iDúsijn\".
  • Tú Mú:...gin þit íswijt, itchijndjn scrips agrívcn djalús in ecnach swif. gin þit íssuifast, nén eidút aneñt isichurnis furgrís in furiphij teghitt ísmnoñ héit. gin þit íslío, minscho íslón, in íschañte we iður fóch, in þurdéns in þurdarcs esís. gin þit íssmeðme, ierhaan ísghitn bi ischiúf fangn nó we iafpit. gin þit íssuiar, íssódjursr teot furiósmnis ísghínit teðm in ifíar eiphij ísghínit teðm.
  • Schen Piú-hsú esés: \"gin þit agrífs nó smeðme þin idúts íochañefañðm in iphlójs echañemacðm.\"

We iléarnin, hénin, fangn, in iriht darcs te bijgrífs, igharin tebhi réghlur emíteghéts, in nídithngwísscho fur iéarme, ametlin.

þurs né grív þits nó ifijf eiméturs sín. Þéðm þitr mógriñðm, þewn; Þéðm þitr nó, þeijtijn.

In se, we plójs dúñphitn, garje itacs eftur tebhi abhíst, véojijeðm we ichañteist fóht.

Gin þit jesés i-ncaghidnis ntach quhit ringur husit, quhit ringurcn déit méar, ibheturs einétchur in eihaan quhit éarm husðm, in quhit losr strangist.

  • Tchauing Jú: Strauing tchérjits, swif hórsís, smeðme sódjurs, schéarp watms - se þit quhin idrumsr bín sceopit þuohíarit, þuobi blijf, in quhin ighóngs gínit irist þuobi radje. Atm þits sibh we isis straing.

Ibhetur léarnt bijgrífs in min quhit husit;

  • Tún Jú:...In se Méstur Wauing esés: \"gin þit ibhijgrífsr nófascht we iséar léarnin þin þuobi fascht in afpitn quhin þurin istúar; gin þit grífsr nó léarnt fúwíó þin ifíar þuohéit iñðm quhin inófrían þurfehtnnðm.

In ighís in plójs quhits gínit in asónseur wij;

  • Tú Mú: Néñðm þemnne bi ermuchuo.

Quhit sijdoñ bi erhaane in quhit sijdoñ bi tiñjt acndjalús.

Gin þit agrív þits hertnin teðm maphlójsis tchést þin 'ssichur þit íown. Cípjeum! Quhin atm þits patchn maphlójsis tchést þin sichur íotijn. Dingijeum!

Quhin iteñts bín pijd te ibheturs emaphlójs, scrips igrív emn mach þitoñ ích teit þurwinin. Bi \"scrips\", þit emn ach swif sibh we quhits betur in furiécwuoécwuo tefauing amtelin.

","title":"Maarcisís Séns: Maarcis' Quotes","translation":"

Don't confuse what you want to be true, with what is true, to do so is delusion. The most bountiful gifts are those given by Fate; race, courage, wisdom, sensibility and the ability to continue on. Loyalty is strongest when shown, not promised. Think twice, speak once. Don't beat a man while he's down, lest he beat you while you're down. Don't trust a man that has opinions about everything. Feel what you feel, but do what you must do. A deed unseen is not a deed undone. Silence breeds suspicion. Beware of the storm in which you see a challenge, it might rob you of your humanly warmth. A knife waved in jest can still cut and stab. If your intelligence is easily offended, then it deserves to be offended. It is foolish to attempt to place fault in a situation in which fault is ultimately irrelevant.  In a case where agency of participants was limited, or where any placement of fault, genuine or not, does not lead to actionable conclusions, then it is a complete waste of time to bother blaming. Ensuring a positive and desired outcome is all that really matters.

","title":"iChañriq þiq Bríghid Schidúñseqiq: An Incantation that Brigid Placed","translation":"

The incantation that Brigid placed, the grace's woman, on the king's white daughter, Gile-Mhin the beauteous. Grace is over you, grace is under you, grace of grace without gainsaying. Excellence of men, excellence of women, excellence of council, excellence of lover, excellence sons and of daughters. Excellence of dells, excellence of knolls, excellence of ravines, excellence of hills. Excellence of travel, excellence of village, excellence of town, excellence of sea and shore. Excellence of beauty, excellence of voice, excellence of skin, excellence of cattle, excellence of butter. You are the night star, you are the brightness of each morning, you are the tidings of each guest, you are the enquiry of every land. You will travel through rough ground, and your feet will not become red. You will travel upwards, and will come back down, you will travel across the sea, and you'll return. You will have no danger, on the knoll or the hill slope, in a ravine or a meadow, on a mountain or in a valley. Not the man, not the woman, not the son, not the daughter. They won't stare nor wish, they won't hate. For anything that would break you, for anything that would lie upon you, for anything that would capture you, for anything that would harm you.

","title":"Luicje Lúgje: Look, O Lugh","translation":"

O Samildánach, O Macnia, O Lonnasclech. Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, no fence, no wall, no fetter restrains you, no blade, no sword, no weapon harms you, no wind, no foot, no chariot surpasses you. Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, no knife, no bullet, no thorn stabs you, no enemy, no soldier, no monster slaughters you, no starvation, no army, no weapon destroys you. Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, for this I pour, for this I ask, for this I pray. Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, Look O Lugh, that I may have your freedom, that I may have your durability, that I may have your speed, that I may have your wisdom, that I may have your breath, that I may have your inflammability, that I may have your thick skin, that I may have your courage, that I may have your strength.

","title":"Bavs Tasén: The Thanking of Badb","translation":"

O Badb, graced Boiling-one. The daring woman so fateful. Your screeching and declaring, crooked she-crow. Your breathing with the eager augur. The battle's righteous and sorrowful willpower. I will address delightful and elegant Badb. You stunned me with a striking dream. You wove sour sights to prophesize. Dark mourning, my disfigured and maimed spirit. That I would unfortunately have, a bad rank. Without daring to do the work. Without a wife or children I would wither most crazily. I must persist, I must fight, a binding omen. A benevolent path, to have a wife and progeny.

Fóht in 1522 in Knockavoe, þiqs anóch þiqs nítste Strabane in Co. Tyrone in Nórn Iȝurln. 'Qwsfóht atwín Claan Ó Domhnaill in Claan Ó Néill. Ó Domhnaills éarmews hídiq bi High Dubh Ó Domhnaill in Manus Ó Domhnaill ísbreður - Hugh Dubh Ó Domhnaills sins. Ó Néills éarmews hídiq bi Conn Bacach Ó Néill. iStúarwsne plóȝq, afruñqiq biq. Ó Néill Ó Domhnaill iqfórlíd ben iniht.

Ó Domhnaill Conn Bacach Ó Néill ewswan fur qeriuing, in se amuchuo éarme eghéðurqȝn fur Tír Conaill qestích - isodȝurs fe Munster, Connacht, MacDonnell fe Antrim, Bissett, MacSheehy in méar þeghéd we Ó Néill, ingoñs sodȝurs ano..

 

Conn Ó Néill in ísmn þechañphiq úqwe Straben. Þursmeðm Hugh Dubh in Manus þeeqoñqðm qe ichañq cwéq se in þestíchiq afruñqiq se. iTwo éarmís þefehtiq ben iniht in ifúmurcnis. Eftur alauing in afúbhluide stúar, Ó Domhnaill iqwn in niȝnhnur iÓ Néillws díd. iChañq Ó Domhnaill iqténiq.

Sicna bro in sicna abhé winin! We is ano atrist Ó Domhnaill iqhudȝn fur qedȝalús quhiq þiq þemndé aneñst iaphoñ þiqws afórðm, fur þiq astúar þudnecnhéȝn iqo we Ó Néill in íséarmís þecheñq, fú se we iChonnacht éarme, þiqws méartchn qe þurlaan, se itchiȝsws se þiq Ó Néill þutstích fur se þiq ewsnístist qeðm, furslóhturq qebhi réðuriñðe, furonibdís in iwaroñd qnófiroñqȝn qewurf þiniq.

Þurhórsís íséarme Ó Domhnaill esés teðm fur qednge, fur þiq nén iwan fur qeaworin fe istúárs tín þehudiq, nó seghn se þiqbauing.

iBhluideist stúar atwín Ó Domhnaill in Ó Néill.

","title":"Zettelkasten S2a: Knockavoes Stúar","translation":"

Fought in 1522 in Knockavoe, a hill near Strabane in Co. Tyrone in Northern Ireland. It was fought between Clan Ó Domhnaill and Clan Ó Néill. Ó Domhnaill's army was led by High Dubh Ó Domhnaill and his brother Manus Ó Domhnaill - Hugh Dubh Ó Domhnaill's sons. Ó Néill's army was led by Conn Bacach Ó Néill. The battle was not planned but a surprise attach. Ó Dómhnaill ambushed Ó Néill at night.

Conn Bacach Ó Néill wanted to rule Ó Domhnaill, and thus gathered a great army to attach Tyrconnell, with soldiers from Munster, Connacht, MacDonnell of Antrim, Bissett, MacSheehy and more went with Ó Néill, as well as English soldiers...

Conn Ó Néill and his man camped outside Strabane. Hugh Dubh and Manus quietly guided their forces to the camp and attacked by surprise. The two armies fought through the night, in the pitch black. After a long and bloody battle, Ó Domhnaill won and nine hundred Ó Néills were dead. Ó Domhnaill took the camp. 

Such a great and astonishing victory! Furthermore, Ó Domhnaill convened to decide what they must do regarding the challenge before them, for they knew they could not win a battle against Ó Néill and his armies, especially as the Connacht army, that was marching to their land, thus the choice was that they would attack Ó Néill for he was closest to them, as they would rather be slaughtered than to become the slave of anyone in the world.

Ó Domhnaill told his army to abandon their horses, for they had no desire to flee the field of battle, unless they were victorious.

The bloodiest battle between Ó Domhnaill and Ó Néill.

Introduction

 

The tribe lived in the highland forests where southern Germany, Czechia, and Austria meet—specifically in the Bavarian and Bohemian Forest regions. Although they were part of the wider Urnfield cultural context, they remained geographically and culturally peripheral. Their way of life was based on transhumance: seasonal movement of livestock between upland summer pastures and lower-elevation wintering grounds. They herded goats, sheep, and small cattle, relying on animals suited to forest-edge and mountain terrain. They practiced a mixed subsistence strategy, combining herding with hunting, foraging, and possibly limited forest-edge horticulture. Wild game such as deer and boar provided meat, while nuts, berries, and roots were gathered from the surrounding woodland. There may have been some slash-and-burn cultivation in open areas, but their lifestyle was not based on intensive agriculture. Their settlements were small, scattered, and temporary—typically consisting of wooden or bark-covered huts reused seasonally. They did not build large permanent structures or fortified hillforts, making them largely invisible in the archaeological record aside from isolated hearths, pits, or tools. Cremation, the hallmark of Urnfield culture, may have been practiced, but likely without formal cemeteries or urnfields. Although isolated, they were aware of and occasionally interacted with surrounding populations. Their main form of contact was through opportunistic raiding of traders moving between the Bohemian Basin (around Plešivec) and the Mur Valley region (Burgstallkogel). They had limited access to bronze tools or ornaments, often acquired through raiding or scavenging. Their language was unique and unwritten, likely a divergent Indo-European variety that retained archaic features due to their isolation. The language spoken by this tribe can be described as an archaic Indo-European offshoot, most closely related to pre-Celtic dialects, with evident structural and lexical connections to Proto-Germanic. It likely diverged from a shared Northwest Indo-European continuum—part of the post-Italo-Celtic and pre-Germanic linguistic zone that developed in Central Europe during the Middle to Late Bronze Age. Due to the tribe’s geographic position in a liminal, upland region and their isolation from denser Urnfield population centers, their language retained older features that had been leveled out in more contact-rich zones. The clearest affinities lie with early Celtic. Their lexicon and morphology shared roots with Lepontic and other pre-Gallic dialects of the eastern Hallstatt zone, particularly in terms related to kinship, pastoralism, and natural features. Phonologically, the language shows signs of early consonantal shifts that anticipate later Germanic changes. For example, voiceless stops may have been lightly fricated in certain environments, a tendency that foreshadows Grimm’s Law. However, the changes were incomplete and inconsistent, suggesting an early divergence from the common Northwest IE stock before full Germanic sound shifts took place. In some lexical sets, shared innovations with Proto-Germanic suggest either a common substrate or prolonged low-level contact in prehistory, possibly via transhumant or seasonal movements that brought neighboring groups into indirect interaction. There are also weaker connections to Proto-Italic and Proto-Balto-Slavic. These are mostly visible in shared conservative features, such as the preservation of laryngeal-influenced vowel coloring . A small number of lexical correspondences suggesting deep-layer areal connections or even older shared inheritance from a pre-divergence Indo-European dialect chain. However, these links are limited and likely reflect distant common ancestry rather than direct contact or recent convergence. In sum, the language represents a conservative, forest-bound offshoot of Northwest Indo-European, most strongly linked to pre-Celtic and early Germanic, but still bearing residual traces of broader Indo-European connections to Italic and Balto-Slavic. Its isolation preserved both old features and early divergent developments, making it an instructive example of how mountainous and forested regions can act as refugia for archaic linguistic forms. This tribe followed a deeply rooted religious tradition shaped by both their Indo-European heritage and the forested, highland environment of the Bavarian and Bohemian regions. At the heart of their belief system was the worship of the Sun, seen as the great divine force that governed life, seasons, and the fate of souls. The Sun was personified as a powerful male being, a chariot-rider and sky-father, who crossed the heavens daily and carried the souls of the dead toward judgment or rebirth. In parallel, the tribe venerated waterways, especially the Vltava and Otava rivers, which they viewed as sacred, living entities. These rivers were believed to connect the world of the living with the Underworld, a deep, dark and cold realm beneath the earth and water where most souls passed after death. Ritual offerings of animal bones, textiles, tools, and carved wooden idols were placed in river currents and forest lakes to appease spirits or guide the dead. Springs and high-altitude lakes were considered portals through which spirits could pass between worlds. A central belief was in reincarnation, that the soul, after death, would travel either into the watery underworld or ascend toward the light, returning to the world of the living in a new form. Ancestors were sometimes thought to return within the same bloodline, especially among those who had died in battle or while hunting. However, not all souls were reborn. The tribe believed that brave warriors, hunters, and clan leaders who died with honor could be chosen by the Sun deity to enter a meadow of heroes, a radiant, far-off land of eternal summer where the sky never darkened. This heroic afterlife was envisioned as a vast plain filled with game, feasting, and battle games, reminiscent of Proto-Indo-European conceptions of a warrior's paradise, later echoed in Celtic and Germanic traditions. Sacred groves played a major role in ritual life. Certain oaks, beeches, or firs were believed to house powerful spirits or serve as pillars connecting the Sky, Earth, and Underworld. Rites were held at these trees to honor the gods, celebrate seasonal cycles, and mark the transitions of birth, death, and rebirth. Trees were never cut in these groves, and their roots were often anointed with milk, blood, or sacred herbs. The tribe maintained a tripartite worldview, inherited from Indo-European tradition: a celestial realm ruled by the solar deity, a middle world of humans and animals, and an underworld of darkness, water, and ancestral spirits. Their oral tradition preserved myths, rituals, and cosmological songs that explained the cycle of life, death, and return. In all, this tribe’s religious life was a synthesis of solar worship, river veneration, forest animism, and a deeply embedded cycle of death and rebirth, with a special destiny reserved for the valorous. Their myths and rites reflected both their environment and their enduring place within the Indo-European spiritual framework.

Proto-Sumro-Donar (PSD) is the ancestor of the Sumro-Donar macro-language family, which is a broad grouping of Sumro-Letaeric and Donorinar languages. PSD is supposed to have existed in the Ancient Age (9000-7001SD), so somewhere between 14,000 and 12,000 years before present. Only a basic grammatical from can be reconstructed for PSD, along with a small glossary of words, but the reconstruction is highly limited by the antiquity of the family. PIF is reconstructed based on Proto-Sumro-Letaeric, a Mythic Age language, and Proto-Donorinar, an Elder Age language, thus the two languages had already been separate for around 3,000 years which highly limits what can be reconstructed. PSD may more accurately serve less as a genuine reconstruction and more as a collection of notes regarding the commonalities between Proto-Sumro-Letaerc and Proto-Donorinar.

The connection between the two language families was first detected not based on a more classic approach of comparative linguistics but thanks to genetic evidence. The idea that Proto-Sumro-Letaeric's deep origins lay with an ancient fishing-based culture far to the south had already been postulated by the notable linguist Sûttörata, the man who reconstructed Proto-Sumro-Letaeric and the father of comparative linguistics. He detected some ancient vocabulary related to fishing, vocabulary that seemed to predate the firmly horticultural economy of the Proto-Sumro-Letaeric speakers. Archaeological evidence did align with this, as the speakers of Proto-Sumro-Letaeric moved into North Makutevnag via the Belt, where they heavily interacted with the Elder Age Sauvatuvar people, adopting horticulture from them and genetically admixing with them. What was not known, however, is just in which lands south of the Belt did the Proto-Sumro-Letaeric speakers originate, and if any of their kind remained. That question is one that was answered by genetics.

The Insular Fishermen were an ancient archaeological culture, dwelling entirely on Donar Island. The Insular Fishermen derive their ancestry from three Primordial Age populations; 74.6% Archaic Fishermen, 23.8% North Monami Hunter-Gatherer and 1.6% Rugged Ridge. The material cultural and lifestyle of the Insular Fishermen show a strong continuity with that of the Archaic Fishermen people who lived along the northern shores of the Monami Sea in Central Makutevnag. This paints a clear picture that the origin of the Proto-Sumro-Letaeric people lie on Donar Island, indeed the modern day inhabitants there show a stronger genetic continuity with the Insular Fishermen.

Ancient Age Ancestry of Elder Age Sumro-Donar speakers.

Ancient Age Ancestry of Mythic Age Sumro-Donar speakers.

Ancient Age Ancestry of Heroic Age Sumro-Donar speakers.

The Donar languages thus became an exciting prospect for discovering the linguistic kin to Proto-Sumro-Letaeric, and so became a topic for study. Proto-Donar was reconstructed with the goal to then see if any possible relation may be found with Proto-Sumro-Letaeric. The two languages weren't found to be incredibly similar, but this was to be expected given the vast amount of time the two had been split apart, but enough core features were identified that allowed the conclusion to be made, with some confidence, that indeed they were related and descend from the language spoken by the Ancient Age Insular Fishermen.

Nouns

Case and Number

Prior to the discovery of the Sumro-Donar macrofamily, the linguist Sûttörata had reconstructed Proto-Sumro-Letaeric with a nominal case system highly reminiscent of later Sumro-Letaeric languages, but he used internal reconstruction to produce an even older and quite pecuilar system, stemming from some stage prior to Proto-Sumro-Letaeric. This remained quite speculative until the relation with Donar languages was discovered, for the nominal system of Donar languages bears strong similarities with that reconstructed by Sûttörata for Pre-Proto-Sumro-Letaeric.

Proto-Donar and Pre-Proto-Sumro-Letaeric are reconstructed as making an "individual" and "non-individual" distinction, where nouns are categorized depending on their relevance as individual objects, which may be singular or plural, vs unenumerated objects which have zero number marking at all. Proto-Sumro-Letaeric instead has animate and inanimate gender system, but this was likely due to influence from Sauvatuvar languages while PSL speakers were in the Belt admixing with those people, whose own languages have animacy gender systems.
