Proto-Donar:

The most notable difference between the two is the lack of the accusative and dative cases in Proto-Donar, for these were likely Proto-Sumro-Letaeric innovations. The individual accusative and dative suffixes appear to have been built upon the genitive, whose suffix is identical to that of Proto-Donar. Proto-Sumro-Letaeric *ǎ is reconstructed as *a in Proto-Sumro-Donar, the backing of the vowel being caused by the vowel *ʌ that was later lost unconditionally. Thus the accusative *-ǎt may be explained as having been *-at-mʌ; *mʌ perhaps being the source of the Proto-Donar *mʌ "direction, way". Originally the accusative would have been a genitive noun followed by the noun *mʌ to give a meaning of "in the direction of X" which later evolved as a way to mark the direct objects of verbs. In a similar fashion the dative may have been *-at-hūʌ, with *hūʌ perhaps being the source of Proto-Donar *hūʌtla "gift", here creating a benefactive construction which later served to become a dative one. Proto-Donar *hū does correspond with Proto-Sumro-Letaeric *w, so perhaps *-at-hūʌ became *-at-wʌ which then had metathesis to become *-awtʌ with the vowel shift of *a triggered by *ʌ, which was then lost resulting, in *-awt. The individual forms of these cases don't bare too much resemblance to the non-individual suffixes which requires extra explanation. Proto-Donar, and its descendants, tend to use different postpositions for individual and non-individual nouns, so this discrepancy could be explained by the cases being the result of different grammaticalised postpositions, built on the non-individual genitive *-ahūʌ. The non-individual accusative *-n may be related to Proto-Donar *nemo "to, at": -ahūʌ-nemo > *-ǎwnemo shortened to *-ǎwn and subsequently *-n. The dative *-ut may come from *-ahūʌ-tos (cf Proto-Donar *tos "for") > *-awtos > *-ut. Proto-Donar seems to be the more conservative with regards to noun case.

With regards to plural marking, however, pre-Proto-Sumro-Letaeric may have been the more archaic. The plural distinction is only made for nominative individual nouns, whereas Proto-Donar makes the distinction for both nominative and genitive. Proto-Donar *-tī appears to have been a result of the nominative plural suffix *-ī being suffixed onto the genitive *-at: *at-ī > *-tī. The loss of the vowel being expected due to Proto-Donar dropping short vowels when the next syllable contains a long vowel.

Proto-Sumro-Donar:

Possessive Suffixes

Proto-Donar has a much simpler set of possessive suffixes, having merely four: *-b for the first person singular and *-t for the second person singular, *-aɣ for the first person plural and *-pū for the second person plural. Proto-Sumro-Letaeric has a more elaborate system:

Proto-Donar lacks any form of agreement between the possesive suffixes and the noun. Proto-Sumro-Letaeric likely gained agreement via influence from the Elder Age Sauvatuvar people, from whom they gained animacy to begin with. The Proto-Sumro-Letaeric inanimate forms may have been innovated using the mysterious R-suffix, while the animate forms were suffixed with the individual genitive suffix *-at. Proto-Donar also lacks possessive suffixes for the third person, as it lacks specific third person pronouns altogether; possession for the third person is marked with the pronoun *siχeʔ "this" with the individual genitive suffix *-at, PSD likely used a similar solution . Proto-Sumro-Letaeric's third person pronouns starting in *m were likely loaned from Sauvatuvar. Another area where Proto-Donar differs from Proto-Sumro-Letaeric is that Proto-Sumro-Letaeric has ambiguity on where a plural possessed noun means that the person is plural or the noun, or both: PD *hōekt-ī-b "my hands" vs *hōekt-pū "our hand" vs  *hōekt-ī-pū "our hands", compare this with PSL *wamar-bat-jeʔ "my relatives, our relative, our relatives".

Pronominals

There is quite some speculation regarding the original natural of Proto-Sumro-Donar pronouns. It is clear from Proto-Donar and pre-Proto-Sumro-Letaeric that there were no third person pronouns at all, their purpose being served by the demonstrative pronoun. There were only the first and second pronouns in both the singular and plural numbers. The speculation is that Proto-Sumro-Donar may at some point, have lacked periphrastic pronouns entirely, even though all descendant language have them.

The hypothesis is that Proto-Sumro-Donar originally had a set of four pronominal morphemes: *-b, *-t,*-aɣ and *-pū which could attach to nouns to mark possession: *hūakuete-t your hand", among other uses. It is thought that the periphrastic pronouns were augmentations of these pronominal affixes. The *-mas- morpheme being the copula *mas "to be" and *-tarɣ being an affix relating to a state of being (cf PSL *-tar "gerund suffix", PSL *-tar in the nominaliser suffixes, PD *-terɣ "derives stative verbs") thus the periphrastic pronoun *bmastarɣ is actually a construction *b-mas-tarɣ "being me, my being". Proto-Sumro-Letaeric seemingly reduced these periphrastic pronouns quite a bit, and later lost the broadly used pronominal affixes. Another thing that suggests that the periphrastic pronouns are derived from the affixes and not vice versa, is that in Proto-Donar, and its daughter languages, periphrastic pronouns remained somewhat of an open class with a variety of pronouns derived with the same pronominal affixes: 

Verbal Morphology

Person

Proto-Donar and Proto-Sumro-Letaeric disagree quite a bit on how they mark person. Proto-Donar marks the first and second person with the pronominal suffixes *-b, *-t,*-aɣ and *-pū, while the third person singular is marked with *-s, likely from *sχē "this, that", and the third person individual plural is marked with *-sī, which is the singular form suffixed with the plural *-ī while there is no plural distinction when agreeing with non-individual nouns. 

Given that the Proto-Donar suffixes have a clear origin from other morphology within the language, while Proto-Sumro-Letaeric's suffixes have no obvious etymology, it is accepted that Proto-Sumro-Letaeric's suffixes are the more archaic, and Proto-Donar is the one that lost the Proto-Sumro-Donar person marking affixes and innovated new ones. Since Proto-Donar can't provide any data for what Proto-Sumro-Donar's person marking suffixes were, we must suffice by reversing the known sound changes to the Proto-Sumro-Letaeric suffixes, accepting that the resulting reconstruction will be quite biased.

Tense

Phonology

Vowels

The vowels consist of a basic five way distinction of /i u e o a/.

Consonants

Syllable Structure

Proto-Horned-Hatchet was completely devoid of any consonant clusters yet very forgiving of vowel hiatuses, with any vowel being able to cluster with any other. Syllables come in two categories, light and heavy. Light syllables are syllables with single vowels while heavy syllables have vowel hiatuses: *haeti "spirit", *ipoe "squirrel", *jokau "to come". There were fairly little rules with regards to restrictions, beyond that the consonants /s r l n/ could not occur word initially.

Prosody

Proto-Horned-Hatched was a stress-timed language. The stress fell on the leftmost heavy syllable in a word: *apepóu "ash", *iwupáe "tough",  *káujopo "maggot". Should a word lack any heavy syllables, then the first syllable bore the stress: *étawi "mother".

Noun Gender and Number

Proto-Horned-Hatchet had a three-way gender system where nouns could either be elder, peer or distant. 

Elder nouns refer to things viewed to be ancestral or of previous familiar generations (*etawi "mother", *tipeho "father", *ekou "grandfather, male ancestor"), as life-giving (*akue "water"), as the source or origin of something else, either as a place or material (*weiphiokha "wood", *ophoe "forest"), as otherwise primordial and cosmic (*pupe "fire", *tokho "mountain", *wasuokho "wind", *eujukha "star", *oakhaukua "sun", *wuetu "moon", *kojoiha "sky", *tikiuthuti "cloud, cosmos, vapour, haze, dream, heavens", *tiulu "god). Elder nouns are made plural by reduplicating the stressed syllable as a suffix: *etawi-e "mother", *tipeho-ti "fathers", *ekou-kou "grandfathers", *tiulu-tiu "gods", *kojoihajoi "skies".

Peer nouns refer to things viewed to be on the same level. This includes familial relatives of the same generation (*tuluiphu "brother", *mesu "sister", *kerapu "wife"), members of ones group (*polako "compatriot"), terrestrial animals which were familiar the Horned Hatchet people, being their common prey or simply often spotted (*ipoe "squirrel", *pako "deer"), man-made items (*posu "hatchet", *jourouphue "spear", *wauphia "pot"). Peer nouns are made plural with the suffix *-hei: *posu-hei "hatchets", *mesu-hei "sisters", *wauphiahei "pots".

Distant nouns refer to things that are spatially distant (*hekhusu "seas", *thari "foreign lands"), people that are outside of one's kin group (*hiuwatu "enemies", *pukhikhae "strangers"), to familial relatives that are of subsequent generations (*pakisa "sons", *tiesaphe "daughters", *wuaphakhu "grandsons"), to hostile animals (*maniesa "leopards"), to aquatic animals, birds and bugs (*apoahio "whales", *pujakhau "crows", *kaujopo "maggots"), to matters relating to death (*moihi "corpses", *pephati "graves", *haeti "spirits"), to hostile weather (*pahi "storms", *makhulo "wildfires"). Distant nouns are peculiar for they are plural by default and are made singular with the suffix *-mu: *pahi-mu "storm", *pakisa-mu "son", *haeti-mu "spirit".

Adjectives

Agreement

Adjectives follow and agree with their nouns. Adjectives agree with singular elder nouns by reduplicating the final syllable as a suffix: *piriu "bright" > *eujukha piriu-riu "bright star", *hipo "small" > *tokho hipo-po "small mountain". Adjectives agree with plural elder nouns by reduplicating the stressed syllable as a suffix which goes after the previously mentioned reduplicated syllable, even if both suffixes are reduplications of the same syllable: *eujukha-eu piriu-riu-riu "bright stars", *tokho-to hipo-po-hi "small mountains".

Adjectives agree with peer nouns by taking on the suffix *-la: *mesu husikhi-la "happy sister", *posu jitirie-la "sharp hatchet". The plural is formed with the suffix *-he after the suffix *-la: *mesu-hei husikhi-la-he "happy sisters", *posu-hei jitirie-la-he "sharp hatchets".

Adjectives agree with distant nouns by taking on the suffix *-(u)ra - the initial vowel is absent when the adjectives ends in u. Like distant nouns, distant adjectives are plural by default: *thari pupho-ura "vast foreign lands", *pakisa tawupu-ra "strong sons". The singular is formed with the suffix *-u: *thari-mu pupho-ura-u "vast foreign land", *pakisa-mu tawupu-ra-u "strong sons"

Pronouns

Verbs

Verbs in Proto-Horned-Hatchet come in two main forms: independent and subordinate. Independent verbs are those which occur in a typical non-subordinated clause e.g "I saw the whale" while subordinate verbs are those which occur inside a subordinate clause e.g "the whale that you saw". 

Semantic Suffixes

Most verbs bear a suffix which specifies which semantic domain the action belongs to. These suffixes can be redundant or derivational in nature.

  1. *-si "verbs of no motion and of state"; *loi-si "to stand" (< *loi "to be")
  2. *-khe "verbs of perception"; *wuphoe-khe "to see" (< *wuphoe "eye")
  3. *-kau "verbs of motion"; *jo-kau "to come" (< *jo "to come")
  4. *-wi "verbs of violence"; *jo-wi "to attack" (< *jo "to come"), *hei-wi "to hunt" (< *hei "hunt")
  5. *-se "verbs of cognition";
  6. *-tha "verbs of consumption";
  7. verbs of emission
  8. verbs of manipulation
  9. verbs of contact
  10. verbs of creation
  11. verbs of transformation
  12. verbs of sound
  13. verbs of illumination
  14. verbs of speech
  15. verbs of possession
  16. verbs of authority
  17. verbs of emotion
  18. verbs of intent

Person and Tense

Proto-Horned-Hatchet verbs agree with their subject by taking on a set of suffixes.

 

Preverbs

Many Proto-Horned-Hatchet verbs bore a prepositional prefix which derived a new meaning from the main verb. 

  • *tawa "out" > *tawa-wuphoe-si "to seem, to appear as, to resemble, to look like" (*wuphoe-khe  "to see")
  • *kau "at" > *kau-jokau "to arrive" (*jokau "to come")
  • *keuka "together with" > *keuka-jokau "to accompany"

Verbs also agree to their object by placing object suffixes after the preverb. The suffixes are as follows.

*keukajokau "to accompany" > *keukane jokaura "I accompany you". When a preverb has an object suffix, it is generally treated as a seperate word from the verb itself

If a verb lacks a preverb, then the dummy preverb *ho- is used: *jowi "to attack" > *hosi jowimu "he attacks them".

Independent vs Subordinate Verbs

Independent verbs consist of the verb root, possibly a preverb, and a suffix marking the semantic category of the action and finally the person and tense marking suffixes. Subordinate verbs consist of the verb root, possibly a preverb, a suffix marking the semantic category of the action, a gerund suffix and no person or tense affixes. Proto-Horned-Hatechet subordinate clauses are verb initial.

The gerund suffix is *-thoi: *jowi "to attack" > *jowithoi "attacking". The subject of subordinate verbs is marked by the preposition *kakhu "by": *jowithoi kakhu khora "that I attack". The object is marked by the possessive particle *keja, the object usually goes after the subject. No tense marking information is used for subordinate verbs, given their fairly nominal nature. The way that subordinate verbs in general function is very ergative-absolutive-like, compared to the nominative-accusative way that independent clauses work.

Noun Gender and Number

Proto-Lion-Headed-Boat had a three-way gender system where nouns could either be elder, peer or distant. 

Elder nouns refer to things viewed to be ancestral or of previous familiar generations (*hitawi "mother", *tipeho "father", *hekou "grandfather, male ancestor"), as life-giving (*ikue "water"), as the source or origin of something else, either as a place or material (*veivioɣa "wood", *ovoe "forest"), as otherwise primordial and cosmic (*pupe "fire", *tuɣo "mountain", *vsuoɣo "wind", *eujuɣa "star", *oaɣaukua "sun", *vuetu "moon", *kojoiha "sky", *tikiuẟuti "cloud, cosmos, vapour, haze, dream, heavens", *tiulu "god). Elder nouns are made plural by reduplicating the stressed syllable as a suffix: *tipeho-ti "fathers", *hekou-kou "grandfathers", *tiulu-tiu "gods", *kojoiha-joi "skies". Sound changes from Proto-Horned-Hatchet to Proto-Lion-headed-Boat have obscured the regular reduplication in some words; words which originally reduplicated a stressed *e *o, later turned *i *u, still reduplicate the vowel as *e *o: *hitawi > *hitawi-e "mothers" (note that word initial epenthetic *h is not reduplicated), this includes instances where the stressed vowel was lost altogether between word initial consonants and fricatives: *tɣo > *tɣo-to "mountains" (< *tuɣo < *tokho ).

Peer nouns refer to things viewed to be on the same level. This includes familial relatives of the same generation (*tuluivu "brother", *msu "sister", *kirapu "wife"), members of ones group (*pulako "compatriot"), terrestrial animals which were familiar the Horned Hatchet people, being their common prey or simply often spotted (*ipoe "squirrel", *pako "deer"), man-made items (*psu "hatchet", *jourouvue "spear", *wauvia "pot"). Peer nouns are made plural with the suffix *-hei: *psu-hei "hatchets", *msu-hei "sisters", *wauviahei "pots". Words which have stressed *i *u from PHH *e *o, shift back to an unstressed *e *o with the application of the suffix *-hei, due to the stress shifting to the suffix: *kirapu > *kerapuhei "wives", *pulako > *polakohei "compatriots".

Distant nouns refer to things that are spatially distant (*heɣusu "seas", *thari "foreign lands"), people that are outside of one's kin group (*hiuwatu "enemies", *pɣiɣae "strangers"), to familial relatives that are of subsequent generations (*pakisa "sons", *tiesave "daughters", *wuavaɣu "grandsons"), to hostile animals (*moniesa "leopards"), to aquatic animals, birds and bugs (*ipoahio "whales", *pujaɣau "crows", *kaujopo "maggots"), to matters relating to death (*moihi "corpses", *pvati "graves", *hieti "spirits"), to hostile weather (*phi "storms", *mɣulo "wildfires"). Distant nouns are peculiar for they are plural by default and are made singular with the suffix *-mu: kaujopo-mu "maggot". Nouns which end in *a *u *i experience a shift to *o *o *e before the suffix *-mu: *phe-mu "storm", *pakiso-mu "son", *hiete-mu "spirit".

Nouns

Athematic

Root final velar plosives become i̯ before endings beginning in consonants: *rḗi̯s "king" (<*rḗg-s) > *riges "king-GEN". Labialised velar plosives become u̯: *óu̯s (> *ókʷ-s) "eye", *wṓu̯s (*wṓkʷ-s) "voice, authority, opinion"

óu̯s "eye" has no plural form, only a dual ending in *-ī, which causes the ó to become ú:  *úkʷī "two eyes". The accusative is *óu̯mo (*ókʷ-m̥ > *ókʷ-mo > *óu-mo).

The word for "foot" is irregular in that the root has the vowel ṓ in the nominative singular and plural (pṓds, pṓdes) but elsewhere has the vowel e: *pédəi, the vowel becomes i should the ending contain e (due to the sound change eCe > iCe): *pídes "foot-GEN" (< *péd-es) but not if the e is a result of a reduplicated vowel after a nasal: *pedme "foot-ACC" (< *péd-m̥). This is a remnant of the older class of athematic acrostatic nouns that were mostly phased out in late PIE, with daughter languages choosing one vowel pattern to be generalizing throughout the whole paradigm cf Latin pēs vs Old English fōt however Proto-Insular stands out for retaining the ablaut in this specific word as an irregular remnant of these acrostatic nouns.
